title: The ramifications of Tadej Pogačar’s Vuelta a España abandonment
content:
Cyclist
The ramifications of Tadej Pogačar’s Vuelta a España abandonment

Suddenly the end of the 2026 season is looking a lot more uncertain than it did a week ago. Tadej Pogačar was predicted by many to win the Vuelta a España, go on to defend his World Championship title and then reign victorious at Il Lombardia for a sixth consecutive year.

Yet a rock in the road reminded us just how fragile expectations can be. One moment Pogačar was leading in Spain, the next he was abandoning a three-week race for the first time in the back of an ambulance, dreams of joining the Grand Tour triple club postponed.

A concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture, stable C7 cervical fracture and multiple abrasions would be the diagnosis. Surgery on the collarbone was initially delayed due to the concussion, but has now been completed successfully with Pogačar now out of hospital and recovering at home.

Right now a timeline for his return is, understandably, less of a priority than his full recovery. As team manager Matxin Joxean Fernandez puts it, ‘the calendar doesn’t matter right now. It’s the person that counts – we have to be there for Tadej. If he needs a rest period, then that’s completely justified. He’s earned it.’

A new rainbow jersey?

As the greatest rider of this generation, there is no surprise that Pogačar has dominated the past two editions of the road race in the World Championships. His first rainbow jersey came in Zurich through a 51km attack to complete the famed Triple Crown as his second was an even lengthier 66km effort in Kigali to claim another gold medal.

But it’s now all but certain that a new name will be on the winner’s list come the 27th September. The Montreal course was designed for a rider like Pogačar – a 272km trip over 12 laps of a punchy parcours that packs in almost 4,000m of elevation. At the moment, the likes of Isaac del Toro (Mexico), Paul Seixas (France), Mathieu van der Poel (Netherlands), Wout van Aert and Remco Evenepoel (Belgium) are all scheduled to make the trip to Canada in what should be an almighty showdown.

No home celebrations

This one is another big blow. The European Championships touch down in Pogačar’s home country of Slovenia from 2-7th October, but any homecoming will surely be on the backburner as he continues to recover from his injuries. A shame given it passes through his hometown of Komenda.

In 2025, Pogačar won his first European championship title after launching an expectantly Pogačaresque 75km solo breakaway for victory ahead of Evenepoel and Seixas. The defending champion is likely to miss out here too as Evenepoel is pencilled in to start.

Il Lombardia record holder hopes nixed… for now

The men’s final Monument of the season in Il Lombardia will take place on the 10th October. This has historically been Pogačar’s playground too, having stood on the top step of the podium for the past five editions. He has this down to a science and typically attacks in the 30km-50km remaining range. Since 2023, this is where he has chosen to end his season with a bang.

However his reign looks set to end in 2026. Just as a Vuelta victory would’ve seen him win every Grand Tour on offer and landed him in a special club, another success at Il Lombardia would’ve made Pogačar the outright win record holder, moving ahead of Fausto Coppi, who also has five victories.

Evenepoel has finished second for the past two editions – just as he placed second to Pogačar in the European Championships last year. He’s had a strong season so far with victory at the Volta Comunitat Valenciana and Amstel Gold Race before coming second to – guess who – at the Tour de France. With a Pogačar-shaped hole for the intermittent future, he might just be the man that stands to gain the most if he seizes the opportunity.

This is cycling though. As we’ve witnessed lately, anything can happen.
